source.title: The Interpolation Phase Transition in Neural Networks: Memorization and Generalization under Lazy Training

record.tranche_reason: The paper reports test-error sweeps around the interpolation threshold using minimum-norm neural tangent regression, a different method and setting from the original deep-network studies.
record.gate_note: The test-error results in Figures 2–4 bear on the claim. The paper also reports interpolation and kernel results, and compares regularized models, but those results do not themselves measure double descent. Values in the figures are not numerically tabulated.
record.test_reason: Section 2.1 and Figure 2 report test error of min-ℓ2-norm neural tangent (NT) regression. They sweep parameter count Nd and sample size n through the interpolation threshold Nd≈n. The paper is not aimed at double descent, and its theory covers only Nd≫n. The numerical sweep is therefore a new-setting result: a linearized random-features model, not a trained deep network. It bears on the general double-descent curve (V4) and on sample-wise non-monotonicity (V3).
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct, with two additions. Numerically, the authors observe that test error blows up at the interpolation threshold Nd≈n and falls as either Nd or n moves away from it. Their theory treats only Nd≫n. There, NT test error approximates infinite-width KRR, which in turn approximates polynomial ridge regression with a self-induced ridge. They conclude that interpolation can be optimal because of this implicit regularization.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes minimum-norm two-layer neural tangent regression with spherical covariates and gives numerical sweeps, rather than reproducing the original deep-network training and measurement setup.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported test-error pattern varies with the relation between parameter count N d and sample size n; the paper's theoretical generalization analysis is restricted to the overparameterized regime.

fits_no_version.finding: The empirical NT kernel becomes nonsingular, and train error vanishes, sharply at Nd/n≈1. Past the threshold, the interpolator behaves like polynomial ridge regression with a positive self-induced ridge term. The authors say interpolation can then be optimal.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In the lazy/NT regime, high-dimensional activation nonlinearity supplies implicit ridge regularization, which explains benign interpolation past the threshold.

record.problems: The numerical illustration fixes d=20 and averages over 10 repetitions; test-error values are presented in plots without numerical tabulation or stated error bars. The theoretical analysis concerns a restricted two-layer neural tangent setting.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-relevant reported results left out.

untested.parts: Model-wise double descent in trained deep networks. Only a linearized NT model is swept through the threshold. The trained two-layer network in Appendix A appears only in the overparametrized regime.
A single effective-complexity measure predicting peak location across axes.
Noise dependence of the peak, multiple peaks, and removal of the peak by optimal regularization. The ridge sweeps in Figures 3–5 lie entirely in the regime Nd≫n, away from the threshold.
Re-counting complexity so that the second descent becomes a U-shaped curve.

missing.what: Train error and kernel singularity versus (Nd, n). Both show the interpolation threshold sits at Nd≈n, which locates the test-error peak.

In the overparametrized regime, test error decays to a limit matching kernel ridge(-less) regression with the infinite-width kernel (Theorem 3.3). The post-peak descent saturates rather than continuing.

record.verdict_notes: Rows are relinked from V1 to V4 because the subject is a linearized random-features model, not a trained deep network. Neither original source applies. The double-descent evidence is a small numerical illustration (d=20, 10 repetitions) with no tabulated values. The paper's theorems do not address the peak itself.

versions.untested_parts: Tested in a numerical two-layer neural tangent setting, not across general deep architectures or nonlinear training regimes.
The reported sample-size/model-size sweep is a numerical illustration in one data setting; broader settings and noise or regularization effects near the threshold are not tested.
Double descent across model classes beyond the neural tangent model.
A single effective-complexity measure predicting peak locations across size, epochs, and sample size.
Whether label noise or variance drives the peak, whether multiple peaks occur, and whether optimal regularization removes it.
Whether an effective parameter count turns the second descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.operation_detail: Swept parameter count N d and sample size n and measured test error.
rows.value: The authors report that test error is large when N d≈n and decreases rapidly as either N d or n moves away from that threshold.
rows.note: The reported pattern is based on a two-dimensional sweep; the figure does not provide numerical test-error values in the text.
rows.check: The model is min-norm NT regression, a linear random-features model, not a trained deep network, so it bears on V4 rather than V1. The V3 link rests on the authors' statement that n and Nd play a 'strikingly symmetric role', with error large at Nd≈n. The rise as n approaches the threshold at fixed Nd is read from the heatmap and that statement; it is not stated as a separate sample-wise curve.

relationships.condition: Min-ℓ2-norm NT (linearized two-layer) regression, d=20, ReLU, σε=0.5, Figure 2
relationships.reason: Test error blows up near Nd≈n and then decreases rapidly as Nd grows, toward the infinite-width KRR risk (r1–r4).
relationships.display_finding: Test error diverged near Nd=n and then decreased rapidly with Nd toward the infinite-width KRR risk.

relationships.condition: Same NT setting, joint (Nd, n) sweep in the Figure 2 heatmap
relationships.reason: The authors describe a symmetric role of n and Nd, with high error at Nd≈n. So increasing n toward the threshold at fixed Nd raises error (r1). This is inferred from the heatmap and the authors' text, not from a dedicated curve.
relationships.display_finding: The reported symmetry between n and Nd, with high error at Nd ≈ n, implies rising error as n approaches fixed Nd.
